You are preparing (NOT executing) a Kubernetes control-plane migration in the repo github.com/maximepatry/k8s-homelab (you are in an isolated git worktree of it). Load the `homelab-engineer` skill first via the Skill tool — it has ground truth on this homelab.

## Goal
Make all repo changes needed to rebuild the cluster with **host2 (10.10.10.20) as the single control-plane** and **host1 (10.10.10.10) + host3 (10.10.10.30) as workers**, on a new local branch `control-plane-host2`. The user will review in the morning and run the rebuild together with the main agent.

## HARD CONSTRAINTS — do not violate
- Do NOT change anything on the live hosts or cluster: no ansible-playbook runs (not even --check is needed; if you run --check, only with --check), no terraform apply/plan against the cluster, no kubectl mutations, no ssh commands that modify state. Read-only ssh/kubectl inspection (`ssh host1 'kubectl get ...'`) is fine. SSH aliases host1/host2/host3 exist in ~/.ssh/config.
- Do NOT git push. Do NOT touch the `main` branch. Commit only on `control-plane-host2`, locally. End commit messages with:
  Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
- Do NOT touch bare-metal/ PXE files (boot.ipxe, dnsmasq, kickstart) except comments/docs — no reinstall is planned, it's a kubeadm-level rebuild on the existing Rocky 9 installs.

## Current state (facts)
- kubeadm 1.31, single control-plane host1, init in `ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml` WITHOUT `--control-plane-endpoint` (API server address = host1 IP baked into certs/kubeconfigs). Workers join via `ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml` using `hostvars['localhost']['kubeadm_join_command']`.
- Inventory: `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` (control_plane: host1; workers: host2, host3; tailscale_router: host1 — KEEP Tailscale on host1, it's independent of control-plane role). Also check group_vars/ (all.yml, control_plane.yml) and host_vars/.
- Nodes register as `hostN.lab.local`. Cilium replaces kube-proxy (`--skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy`), so Cilium's `k8sServiceHost` must point at the API endpoint — it's set in `terraform/cluster-bootstrap` (helm_release.cilium, bootstrap-only — DO NOT remove that resource) AND in `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/cilium.yml` (ArgoCD adopts the same release). Both must agree.
- An uncommitted change exists in the MAIN working tree (not your worktree) at /Users/maximepatry/projects/k8s-homelab/ansible/roles/kubeadm/tasks/main.yml: two tasks that write `/etc/sysconfig/kubelet` with `KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--node-ip={{ ansible_host }}` and restart kubelet when changed. It was already applied live and fixes a real bug (host3 moved to a USB NIC and kubelet auto-picked a Cilium IP). Copy that change into your branch (read the file from the main tree path) and keep it.
- host3 now uses a USB 2.5/1GbE adapter (NetworkManager profile `usb-eth`, MAC c8:a3:62:a1:cb:1d) because its onboard enp2s0 only negotiates 100 Mb/s. `ansible/inventory/host_vars/host3.yml` and README still say "100 Mb/s, fix the cable" — update those comments to reflect the USB adapter fix (onboard port faulty; PXE reinstall still goes through onboard enp2s0).

## What to implement
1. Inventory: host2 → control_plane, host1 + host3 → workers. Tailscale stays on host1.
2. kubeadm init with a stable `--control-plane-endpoint` so future control-plane moves don't need a rebuild. Recommended: a DNS name like `k8s-api.lab.local:6443` resolved via an /etc/hosts entry managed by Ansible on all nodes (common role), pointing to the control-plane IP (derive from inventory, don't hardcode), plus `--apiserver-cert-extra-sans` for the IP and name. Pass `--apiserver-advertise-address={{ ansible_host }}`. If you think kube-vip (static-pod VIP) is clearly better, you may implement it instead but justify it in the commit message — keep it simple, this is a learning homelab. The Mac also needs to reach the endpoint (kubeconfig fetched to the repo) — note in docs that the Mac needs the same /etc/hosts entry, or use the IP in the fetched kubeconfig, your call; be explicit.
3. Update everything that hardcodes 10.10.10.10 / host1 as the API server: Cilium k8sServiceHost (terraform + ArgoCD values), terraform providers/kubeconfig paths, any MetalLB/ingress/Homepage config that assumes host1 is control-plane, node labels/taints logic in roles. grep the whole repo (`10.10.10.10`, `host1`, `control_plane`, `k8sServiceHost`, `6443`).
4. Decide whether host2 (Intel N150, 4c/4t, 16 GB — the weakest node) should be tainted NoSchedule as a dedicated control-plane. The user's intent: host1/host3 have more power and should run workloads. Default to tainting host2 (i.e. don't remove the standard control-plane taint), and make sure system DaemonSets still run there. If anything in the repo removes the control-plane taint for host1 today, adjust it.
5. Update docs (README.md, the homelab-engineer skill at .claude/skills/homelab-engineer/SKILL.md, ansible comments) to the new topology. Docs in bare-metal/ are in French — match that. Do NOT write the step-by-step runbook — another agent is doing that; just make the code + reference docs correct.
6. Run `ansible-playbook --syntax-check` and `terraform validate` (in terraform/cluster-bootstrap, `terraform init -backend=false` if needed) — these are local-only and safe. Fix what fails.

## Report back (concise)
- Branch name, worktree path, list of commits.
- Every file changed with a one-line why.
- Exact list of anything you were unsure about or deliberately left alone (e.g., values you could not verify), and anything the rebuild operator must do manually (e.g., Mac /etc/hosts).
- Results of syntax-check / validate.

Only a SubagentHandback call reaches your caller as your result; plain text you write at the end is not delivered. Do not also send the report with SendMessage: your caller would get it twice.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/maximepatry/projects/k8s-homelab/.claude/skills/homelab-engineer

# Homelab engineer

## Role

Operate as a senior cloud/DevOps engineer working in this specific repo, not
a generic assistant. That means:

- **Verify before you assert.** Don't guess IPs, MACs, or host state from
  memory — `bare-metal/hosts.csv` is the single source of truth for the
  inventory. If something in the repo looks inconsistent with what's below,
  say so explicitly rather than silently picking one.
- **Treat production hosts as production.** These are real machines with
  real disks. `rootpw --lock` + key-only SSH + wheel NOPASSWD sudo is the
  standing security posture — don't propose password auth, root login, or
  loosening sudo as a "quick fix."
- **Respect the PXE reinstall hazard.** `boot.ipxe` has no "already
  installed" guard — anything that PXE-boots and matches a MAC in the
  dispatch table gets wiped and reinstalled via kickstart. Before touching
  `boot.ipxe`, `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`, or a host's boot order, check
  whether that host is already provisioned (see inventory below) and warn
  the user if a change could trigger an unintended reinstall. See
  `bare-metal/README.md` for the comment-vs-delete convention used once a
  host is confirmed installed.
- **Prefer changes that go through the repo, not one-off SSH sessions.**
  This is an IaC-managed homelab: kickstart files, dnsmasq config, and
  `deploy-opal.sh` are the source of truth for the Opal and the hosts, not
  whatever's live on the router right now. If you SSH in to fix something
  ad hoc, also update the corresponding file in the repo and redeploy, or
  flag clearly that you didn't.
- **Flag stale docs instead of trusting them.** This repo was originally
  scaffolded as a Proxmox VE + Terraform + kubeadm template. That design was
  abandoned in favor of bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 (see "History" below). The
  top-level `README.md` and `docs/` have been corrected to reflect this
  (real hardware, real IPs, real topology) — the two Proxmox-era command
  files that used to describe the old architecture were deleted, not
  updated. If a doc still mentions Proxmox, `192.168.1.x`, or `rocky`/
  `ubuntu` as the SSH user outside of historical "here's what changed"
  context, it's stale — fix it or flag it, don't trust it.
- **ArgoCD syncs from the GitHub remote, not local files.** Any change
  under `clusters/homelab/` or `apps/` does nothing until it's committed
  *and pushed* to `main` — editing locally and expecting the cluster to
  react is a common mistake here (bit during the initial bootstrap: two
  Applications failed and Cilium briefly ran with stale values because
  nothing had been pushed yet).

## Current infrastructure (ground truth)

### Fleet

Three bare-metal mini PCs, **all running Rocky Linux 9** installed via PXE +
kickstart. No hypervisor anywhere.

| Host  | IP           | MAC               | Notes |
|-------|--------------|-------------------|-------|
| host1 | 10.10.10.10  | 78:55:36:02:de:9e | Kubernetes control-plane (untainted, also schedulable). Strongest node — Ryzen 7 6800H, 32GB, 1TB NVMe — see README hardware table, polled live 2026-08-11. |
| host2 | 10.10.10.20  | e8:ff:1e:d8:a0:d0 | Kubernetes worker. First host provisioned; PXE dispatch commented out in `boot.ipxe` post-install. Intel N150, 16GB — lightest node. |
| host3 | 10.10.10.30  | 00:16:96:ee:1e:4d | Kubernetes worker. Ryzen 7 5800H, 32GB — mid-pack, not "the beefiest" (that was a wrong assumption before hardware was actually polled; host1 is stronger). NIC currently links at only 100 Mb/s — check the cable/switch port before relying on this node for anything throughput-sensitive. |

kubelet registers each node under its OS hostname (`hostN.lab.local`, from the kickstart), not the bare
`hostN` — `kubectl get nodes` shows `host1.lab.local` etc., and any `kubectl label`/`taint` command needs
the `.lab.local` suffix.

Source of truth: `bare-metal/hosts.csv`. If you change an IP or MAC, update
that file, the matching `dhcp-host` line in
`bare-metal/router/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`, and the matching `iseq` block
in `bare-metal/router/boot.ipxe` together — they have to stay in sync
manually, nothing enforces it.

### Access

- SSH user: `foo`. Root login is locked (`rootpw --lock`). Key-only auth,
  no password fallback.
- Default key: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab`. If a plain `ssh foo@<host>`
  prompts for a password, it's almost always the client not picking up this
  non-default key name — use `-i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab` or add an SSH
  config `Host` block, don't assume the host is misconfigured.
- Passwordless sudo via `/etc/sudoers.d/wheel-nopasswd` (`%wheel ALL=(ALL)
  NOPASSWD: ALL`), set in each kickstart's `%post`.
- Hostnames are `hostN.lab.local`; there's no working DNS for these outside
  the provisioning subnet, use the IPs.

### Network

- Provisioning/production LAN: `10.10.10.0/24`.
- Gateway / DHCP+TFTP+PXE server: `10.10.10.1` — a GL.iNet Opal (GL-SFT1200)
  travel router repurposed as an isolated provisioning appliance. Its WAN
  side uplinks to the home network for internet access during installs.
  Admin/LuCI-equivalent access and the deploy script both go through this
  IP.
- This is a deliberately isolated subnet, not the user's main home LAN. A
  WireGuard tunnel (`wg_mgmt` interface on the Opal, UDP port 51821 —
  deliberately different from GL.iNet's own unused native WireGuard-server
  feature on port 51820) now bridges the Mac jumpbox into `10.10.10.0/24`
  from the home LAN — see `bare-metal/README.md`, "Tunnel WireGuard pour le
  jumpbox". The Opal's dropbear SSH server has no Ed25519 support (confirmed
  by testing — only RSA works for admin SSH to the Opal itself, separate
  from the Ed25519 key used for the Rocky hosts).

### Provisioning pipeline (bare-metal/)

```
bare-metal/
├── hosts.csv                          # hostname/MAC/IP source of truth
├── router/
│   ├── dnsmasq-provisioning.conf      # DHCP reservations + iPXE chainload
│   ├── boot.ipxe                      # MAC → kickstart dispatch
│   └── deploy-opal.sh                 # pushes config to the Opal over SSH
├── kickstart/
│   ├── ks-host1.cfg
│   ├── ks-host2.cfg
│   └── ks-host3.cfg
└── README.md                          # full write-up, read this for detail
```

Flow: host PXE-boots → Opal's dnsmasq recognizes its MAC and chainloads
iPXE → iPXE (`boot.ipxe`) matches the MAC and fetches the matching kernel/
initrd from the official Rocky mirror plus that host's kickstart from
`raw.githubusercontent.com` (repo must stay **public** — Anaconda has no
way to auth) → Anaconda partitions, sets hostname/static IP, installs
packages, runs `%post`.

Two things that bite people working on this pipeline:

1. **UEFI vs BIOS PXE binaries.** All three hosts are UEFI. The Opal serves
   `snponly.efi` (saved locally as `ipxe.efi`), not `undionly.kpxe` — the
   BIOS-legacy binary downloads fine over TFTP on UEFI firmware but silently
   fails to execute, which looks like "PXE just doesn't do anything."
2. **dnsmasq confdir is tmpfs.** On this firmware, `/tmp/dnsmasq.d` is
   wiped on every reboot. The real config lives in
   `/etc/dnsmasq.d/provisioning.conf` and gets re-mirrored into
   `/tmp/dnsmasq.d` by an `/etc/rc.local` hook. Any manual edit on the
   router that isn't also made in the repo (and redeployed via
   `deploy-opal.sh`) will disappear on next reboot.

Redeploying after any change to `router/*`: `./bare-metal/router/deploy-opal.sh 10.10.10.1`.

Full narrative and troubleshooting history: `bare-metal/README.md`.

### Kubernetes cluster — built and running (as of 2026-08-11)

`terraform/proxmox/` is gone (deleted, replaced by `terraform/cluster-bootstrap/` — see below).
`ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` points at the real bare-metal IPs. The cluster is live:

- kubeadm 1.31, host1 = control-plane (untainted/schedulable — it's the strongest node, not just an etcd
  appliance), host2 + host3 = workers. `ansible-playbook playbooks/bootstrap.yml` is fully idempotent —
  safe to rerun, 0 changes expected on a healthy cluster.
- Cilium is installed **twice, deliberately**: once via `terraform/cluster-bootstrap`'s
  `helm_release.cilium` (bootstrap-only, breaks the chicken-and-egg problem where ArgoCD's own pods can't
  schedule without a CNI — Cilium's agent DaemonSet uses `hostNetwork: true` so it alone can start before
  any CNI exists), and then ArgoCD adopts/reconciles the same Helm release going forward via
  `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/cilium.yml`. Don't "clean up" the Terraform `helm_release.cilium`
  resource thinking it's redundant with ArgoCD's Application — removing it would `helm uninstall` Cilium
  out from under the cluster.
- ArgoCD, once past that bootstrap step, owns everything else: `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/`
  (MetalLB + `metallb-pool` IPAddressPool, cert-manager, ingress-nginx, Longhorn) and `apps/prod`/
  `apps/stage` (empty scaffolds — no real workloads deployed yet).
- **ArgoCD only syncs from the actual GitHub remote (`main`), never a local working copy** — this bit
  during the initial bootstrap (apps-prod/apps-stage failed with "app path does not exist", Cilium ran
  briefly with a stale `k8sServiceHost` value) until everything was committed and pushed. Any future
  change to `clusters/homelab/` or `apps/` needs to reach GitHub before ArgoCD will act on it — editing
  local files alone does nothing.
- Longhorn storage: no host has a second disk (see hardware table) — an Ansible `storage` role role
  (`ansible/roles/storage/`) carves an LV out of each host's free LVM space and mounts it at
  `/var/lib/longhorn` before Kubernetes/Longhorn ever sees it.

If the cluster ever looks broken/missing, verify against real state (`kubectl get nodes`,
`kubectl -n argocd get applications`) before assuming — don't trust this note's timestamp blindly for
anything time-sensitive (node health, sync status, chart versions).

### History (why bare-metal, not Proxmox)

The repo was originally templated for Proxmox VE on every node with K8s
running in VMs. That was tried on host1/host3; the Proxmox auto-installer's
netboot path (large initrd, needed local USB staging on the Opal, more
failure modes) proved more fragile than Rocky/Anaconda's kickstart path.
All three hosts were consolidated onto bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 instead —
simpler, and the PXE pipeline above is fully IaC-driven with no local
staging on the Opal's 128MB flash. Media-server use cases were also dropped;
current intent is a Kubernetes learning environment for certification
study. A later idea to swap Rocky for Talos OS was considered and shelved
("on reste sur Rocky pour le moment") — if it resurfaces, use the real
topology below (host1 as control-plane), not an assumption.

## Working conventions

- Repo: `github.com/maximepatry/k8s-homelab`, public (required for
  `raw.githubusercontent.com` kickstart fetches — don't suggest making it
  private without calling out that this breaks provisioning).
- Primary language for docs/comments in `bare-metal/` is French — match it
  when editing files there unless told otherwise.
- When you change host-facing config (kickstart, dnsmasq, boot.ipxe),
  always name the exact host(s) affected and whether a redeploy or reinstall
  is required — never leave that implicit.

=== ansible/playbooks/bootstrap.yml
---
- name: Common setup on all nodes
  hosts: k8s_cluster
  roles:
    - role: common
      tags: common
    - role: storage
      tags: storage
    - role: containerd
      tags: containerd
    - role: kubeadm
      tags: kubeadm

- name: Initialize control plane
  hosts: control_plane
  roles:
    - role: control-plane
      tags: control-plane

- name: Join workers
  hosts: workers
  roles:
    - role: worker
      tags: worker
=== ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  # No --cluster-name flag exists on `kubeadm init` (it's a ClusterConfiguration
  # field, only settable via --config) - naming the cluster would need a full
  # kubeadm config file for one cosmetic value, not worth it here.
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for foo user
  file:
    path: /home/foo/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: foo
    group: foo

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/foo/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: foo
    group: foo
    mode: "0600"

- name: Fetch kubeconfig to local machine
  # playbook_dir is ansible/playbooks/ - need two levels up to reach the
  # repo root, not one (this previously landed at ansible/clusters/... and
  # was never actually used by Terraform/kubectl at the documented path).
  fetch:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    flat: true

- name: Restrict local kubeconfig permissions
  file:
    path: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    mode: "0600"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false

- name: Generate join command
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true

# host1 is the strongest node in this fleet (Ryzen 7 6800H, 1TB NVMe) -
# don't waste its capacity on etcd alone. Untainting is normal practice
# for a single-control-plane homelab cluster.
#
# kubelet registers the node under its OS hostname (kickstart sets
# `hostN.lab.local`, not the bare `hostN` used as the Ansible inventory
# name) - {{ inventory_hostname }} alone does not match any real node and
# silently no-ops here.
- name: Remove control-plane NoSchedule taint so this node is schedulable
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    taint nodes {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule-
  register: untaint_result
  changed_when: "'untainted' in untaint_result.stdout"
  failed_when: untaint_result.rc != 0 and 'not found' not in untaint_result.stderr
=== ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Check if node is already joined
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
  register: kubelet_conf

- name: Join cluster
  command: "{{ hostvars['localhost']['kubeadm_join_command'] }}"
  when: not kubelet_conf.stat.exists

- name: Label node as worker
  # kubelet registers under the OS hostname (hostN.lab.local from
  # kickstart), not the bare inventory_hostname - see the matching note in
  # control-plane/tasks/main.yml.
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /home/foo/.kube/config
    label node {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=worker --overwrite
  delegate_to: "{{ groups['control_plane'][0] }}"
  become: false
=== ansible/roles/common/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Install base packages
  dnf:
    name:
      - curl
      - ca-certificates
      - gnupg2
      - iscsi-initiator-utils   # required by Longhorn
      - nfs-utils               # required by Longhorn
      - iproute-tc              # required by Cilium
      - conntrack-tools         # required by kubeadm preflight checks
    state: present

- name: Enable and start iscsid
  systemd:
    name: iscsid
    enabled: true
    state: started

- name: Disable swap
  command: swapoff -a
  when: ansible_swaptotal_mb > 0

- name: Remove swap from fstab
  lineinfile:
    path: /etc/fstab
    regexp: '\sswap\s'
    state: absent

- name: Disable zram-generator (Rocky Linux 9 swap via zram)
  systemd:
    name: "{{ item }}"
    enabled: false
    state: stopped
    masked: true
  loop:
    - swap.target
  ignore_errors: true

- name: Load required kernel modules
  modprobe:
    name: "{{ item }}"
    state: present
  loop:
    - overlay
    - br_netfilter

- name: Persist kernel modules
  copy:
    dest: /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
    content: |
      overlay
      br_netfilter

- name: Set sysctl params for k8s networking
  sysctl:
    name: "{{ item.key }}"
    value: "{{ item.value }}"
    sysctl_file: /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
    reload: true
  loop:
    - { key: net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables,  value: "1" }
    - { key: net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables, value: "1" }
    - { key: net.ipv4.ip_forward,                 value: "1" }

=== ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  # No --cluster-name flag exists on `kubeadm init` (it's a ClusterConfiguration
  # field, only settable via --config) - naming the cluster would need a full
  # kubeadm config file for one cosmetic value, not worth it here.
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for foo user
  file:
    path: /home/foo/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: foo
    group: foo

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/foo/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: foo
    group: foo
    mode: "0600"

- name: Fetch kubeconfig to local machine
  # playbook_dir is ansible/playbooks/ - need two levels up to reach the
  # repo root, not one (this previously landed at ansible/clusters/... and
  # was never actually used by Terraform/kubectl at the documented path).
  fetch:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    flat: true

- name: Restrict local kubeconfig permissions
  file:
    path: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    mode: "0600"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false

- name: Generate join command
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true

# host1 is the strongest node in this fleet (Ryzen 7 6800H, 1TB NVMe) -
# don't waste its capacity on etcd alone. Untainting is normal practice
# for a single-control-plane homelab cluster.
#
# kubelet registers the node under its OS hostname (kickstart sets
# `hostN.lab.local`, not the bare `hostN` used as the Ansible inventory
# name) - {{ inventory_hostname }} alone does not match any real node and
# silently no-ops here.
- name: Remove control-plane NoSchedule taint so this node is schedulable
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    taint nodes {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule-
  register: untaint_result
  changed_when: "'untainted' in untaint_result.stdout"
  failed_when: untaint_result.rc != 0 and 'not found' not in untaint_result.stderr
=== ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Check if node is already joined
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
  register: kubelet_conf

- name: Join cluster
  command: "{{ hostvars['localhost']['kubeadm_join_command'] }}"
  when: not kubelet_conf.stat.exists

- name: Label node as worker
  # kubelet registers under the OS hostname (hostN.lab.local from
  # kickstart), not the bare inventory_hostname - see the matching note in
  # control-plane/tasks/main.yml.
  command: >

  delegate_to: "{{ groups['control_plane'][0] }}"
  become: false

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: longhorn
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://charts.longhorn.io
    chart: longhorn
    targetRevision: "1.7.*"
    helm:
      valuesObject:
        defaultSettings:
          defaultReplicaCount: 2
          storageMinimalAvailablePercentage: 10
        persistence:
          defaultClass: true
          defaultClassReplicaCount: 2
        preUpgradeChecker:
          # The chart's own docs recommend this for ArgoCD/GitOps installs:
          # the pre-upgrade check is a PreSync hook Job that assumes the
          # longhorn-service-account it runs as already exists - true on a
          # real `helm upgrade`, not on ArgoCD's first sync of a fresh
          # install (PreSync hooks run before the regular Sync-phase
          # ServiceAccount, so the Job can never actually schedule). The
          # Application-level `SkipHooks=true` syncOption does not actually
          # work around this in the ArgoCD version this cluster runs
          # (v2.13.4 - the option is accepted but silently has no effect),
          # so disable the hook at the chart level instead.
          jobEnabled: false
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: longhorn-system
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: monitoring
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
    chart: kube-prometheus-stack
    targetRevision: "88.*"
    helm:
      # The Prometheus Operator CRDs (Prometheus, Alertmanager, etc.) have
      # OpenAPI schemas large enough that client-side apply's
      # kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation exceeds
      # Kubernetes' 262144-byte annotation limit - a well-known
      # kube-prometheus-stack + ArgoCD gotcha. Neither the Application-level
      # `ServerSideApply=true` syncOption nor `Replace=true` actually fixed
      # this on this cluster (confirmed: ArgoCD's CRD apply path doesn't
      # honor ServerSideApply, and Replace is disabled server-side on this
      # ArgoCD install) - a plain `kubectl apply --server-side` on the same
      # CRD works fine, proving it's an ArgoCD-specific limitation, not a
      # real size problem. Fix: skip CRD management here entirely and
      # apply all 10 CRDs once, manually, via server-side apply - see
      # docs/monitoring.md, "Installing/upgrading the CRDs" for the exact
      # command. Re-run it after bumping targetRevision to a version with
      # CRD changes.
      skipCrds: true
      valuesObject:
        # By default this chart's admission webhook TLS cert is generated
        # by a PreSync hook Job (kube-webhook-certgen) - the exact pattern
        # that hit a fast-reconcile loop with ingress-nginx on this cluster
        # (see clusters/homelab/infrastructure/ingress-nginx.yml) and never
        # got a chance to complete. cert-manager is already running here,
        # so use it instead and skip the Job-based path entirely.
        prometheusOperator:
          admissionWebhooks:
            certManager:
              enabled: true

        # kubeadm binds controller-manager/scheduler/etcd to 127.0.0.1 by
        # default - Prometheus (running in a pod) can never reach those
        # targets, they'd just sit permanently "down". kube-proxy doesn't
        # run at all (Cilium replaces it, kubeadm init --skip-phases=
        # addon/kube-proxy) - scraping it would 100% fail too. Disable all
        # four rather than ship known-broken targets.
        kubeControllerManager:
          enabled: false
        kubeScheduler:
          enabled: false
        kubeEtcd:
          enabled: false
        kubeProxy:
          enabled: false

        prometheus:
          prometheusSpec:
            retention: 15d
            storageSpec:
              volumeClaimTemplate:
                spec:
                  storageClassName: longhorn
                  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
                  resources:
                    requests:
                      storage: 20Gi

        alertmanager:
          alertmanagerSpec:
            storage:
              volumeClaimTemplate:
                spec:
                  storageClassName: longhorn
                  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
                  resources:
                    requests:
                      storage: 5Gi

        grafana:
          # adminPassword intentionally not set - the chart auto-generates
          # one into a Secret (admin-user/admin-password keys) rather than
          # this being a plaintext value in a public repo. See
          # docs/monitoring.md for how to retrieve it.
          persistence:
            enabled: true
            type: sts
            storageClassName: longhorn
            accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
            size: 5Gi
          ingress:
            enabled: true
            ingressClassName: nginx
            # TLS via the internal homelab CA (clusters/homelab/infrastructure/
            # cert-manager-ca) - not Let's Encrypt, homelab.local isn't a real
            # domain. See docs/networking.md, "Trusting the homelab CA".
            annotations:
              cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: homelab-ca
            hosts:
              - grafana.homelab.local
            path: /
            tls:
              - secretName: grafana-tls
                hosts:
                  - grafana.homelab.local
          # sidecar.dashboards is already enabled by chart default (watches
          # ConfigMaps labeled grafana_dashboard=1 in any namespace) - the
          # custom dashboard lives in monitoring-dashboards.yml alongside
          # this file.
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: longhorn
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://charts.longhorn.io
    chart: longhorn
    targetRevision: "1.7.*"
    helm:
      valuesObject:
        defaultSettings:
          defaultReplicaCount: 2
          storageMinimalAvailablePercentage: 10
        persistence:
          defaultClass: true
          defaultClassReplicaCount: 2
        preUpgradeChecker:
          # The chart's own docs recommend this for ArgoCD/GitOps installs:
          # the pre-upgrade check is a PreSync hook Job that assumes the
          # longhorn-service-account it runs as already exists - true on a
          # real `helm upgrade`, not on ArgoCD's first sync of a fresh
          # install (PreSync hooks run before the regular Sync-phase
          # ServiceAccount, so the Job can never actually schedule). The
          # Application-level `SkipHooks=true` syncOption does not actually
          # work around this in the ArgoCD version this cluster runs
          # (v2.13.4 - the option is accepted but silently has no effect),
          # so disable the hook at the chart level instead.
          jobEnabled: false
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: longhorn-system
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: monitoring
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
    chart: kube-prometheus-stack
    targetRevision: "88.*"
    helm:
      # The Prometheus Operator CRDs (Prometheus, Alertmanager, etc.) have
      # OpenAPI schemas large enough that client-side apply's
      # kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation exceeds
      # Kubernetes' 262144-byte annotation limit - a well-known
      # kube-prometheus-stack + ArgoCD gotcha. Neither the Application-level
      # `ServerSideApply=true` syncOption nor `Replace=true` actually fixed
      # this on this cluster (confirmed: ArgoCD's CRD apply path doesn't
      # honor ServerSideApply, and Replace is disabled server-side on this
      # ArgoCD install) - a plain `kubectl apply --server-side` on the same
      # CRD works fine, proving it's an ArgoCD-specific limitation, not a
      # real size problem. Fix: skip CRD management here entirely and
      # apply all 10 CRDs once, manually, via server-side apply - see
      # docs/monitoring.md, "Installing/upgrading the CRDs" for the exact
      # command. Re-run it after bumping targetRevision to a version with
      # CRD changes.
      skipCrds: true
      valuesObject:
        # By default this chart's admission webhook TLS cert is generated
        # by a PreSync hook Job (kube-webhook-certgen) - the exact pattern
        # that hit a fast-reconcile loop with ingress-nginx on this cluster
        # (see clusters/homelab/infrastructure/ingress-nginx.yml) and never
        # got a chance to complete. cert-manager is already running here,
        # so use it instead and skip the Job-based path entirely.
        prometheusOperator:
          admissionWebhooks:
            certManager:
              enabled: true

        # kubeadm binds controller-manager/scheduler/etcd to 127.0.0.1 by
        # default - Prometheus (running in a pod) can never reach those
        # targets, they'd just sit permanently "down". kube-proxy doesn't
        # run at all (Cilium replaces it, kubeadm init --skip-phases=
        # addon/kube-proxy) - scraping it would 100% fail too. Disable all
        # four rather than ship known-broken targets.
        kubeControllerManager:
          enabled: false
        kubeScheduler:
          enabled: false
        kubeEtcd:
          enabled: false
        kubeProxy:
          enabled: false

        prometheus:
          prometheusSpec:
            retention: 15d
            storageSpec:
              volumeClaimTemplate:
                spec:
                  storageClassName: longhorn
                  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
                  resources:
                    requests:
                      storage: 20Gi

        alertmanager:
          alertmanagerSpec:
            storage:
              volumeClaimTemplate:
                spec:
                  storageClassName: longhorn
                  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
                  resources:
                    requests:
                      storage: 5Gi

        grafana:
          # adminPassword intentionally not set - the chart auto-generates
          # one into a Secret (admin-user/admin-password keys) rather than
          # this being a plaintext value in a public repo. See
          # docs/monitoring.md for how to retrieve it.
          persistence:
            enabled: true
            type: sts
            storageClassName: longhorn
            accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
            size: 5Gi
          ingress:
            enabled: true
            ingressClassName: nginx
            # TLS via the internal homelab CA (clusters/homelab/infrastructure/
            # cert-manager-ca) - not Let's Encrypt, homelab.local isn't a real
            # domain. See docs/networking.md, "Trusting the homelab CA".
            annotations:
              cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: homelab-ca
            hosts:
              - grafana.homelab.local
            path: /
            tls:
              - secretName: grafana-tls
                hosts:
                  - grafana.homelab.local
          # sidecar.dashboards is already enabled by chart default (watches
          # ConfigMaps labeled grafana_dashboard=1 in any namespace) - the
          # custom dashboard lives in monitoring-dashboards.yml alongside
          # this file.
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc

/bin/cat >> ansible/inventory/group_vars/all.yml <<'EOF'

# Stable Kubernetes API endpoint (kubeadm --control-plane-endpoint). Baked
# into every cert/kubeconfig at `kubeadm init` time as a NAME, not host2's IP,
# so the control-plane can later move to another node by repointing this name
# (the /etc/hosts entry written by the common role) instead of rebuilding the
# cluster. The IP is derived from the inventory - whichever host is first in
# the control_plane group - never hardcoded here.
#
# Two consumers can't resolve this name and use the IP directly instead (keep
# them in sync with the control_plane group by hand):
#   - Cilium's k8sServiceHost (terraform/cluster-bootstrap/main.tf AND
#     clusters/homelab/infrastructure/cilium.yml)
#   - the kubeconfig fetched to the Mac (clusters/homelab/kubeconfig), which
#     the control-plane role rewrites to the IP so the Mac needs no
#     /etc/hosts entry
control_plane_endpoint_name: k8s-api.lab.local
control_plane_endpoint_port: 6443
control_plane_ip: "{{ hostvars[groups['control_plane'][0]]['ansible_host'] }}"
control_plane_endpoint: "{{ control_plane_endpoint_name }}:{{ control_plane_endpoint_port }}"
EOF
/bin/cat > ansible/inventory/hosts.yml <<'EOF'
all:
  children:
    # host2 (Intel N150, 4c/4t, 16 GB) is the dedicated control-plane: it's
    # the lightest node, and keeping the standard control-plane NoSchedule
    # taint frees host1/host3 (both 8c/16t Ryzen, 32 GB) for workloads. The
    # API server is reached through control_plane_endpoint (group_vars/
    # all.yml), not this IP, so this group can change without a rebuild.
    control_plane:
      hosts:
        host2:
          ansible_host: 10.10.10.20

    workers:
      hosts:
        host1:
          ansible_host: 10.10.10.10
        host3:
          ansible_host: 10.10.10.30

    k8s_cluster:
      children:
        control_plane:
        workers:

    # Tailscale subnet router for 10.10.10.0/24 — deliberately host1, not the
    # GL.iNet Opal (128MB RAM/flash, Siflower SoC, package support uncertain).
    # See bare-metal/README.md, "Tailscale". Independent of control_plane
    # membership — host1 is a worker now and keeps this role; don't assume
    # the control-plane node gets it.
    tailscale_router:
      hosts:
        host1:
EOF
/bin/cat > ansible/inventory/host_vars/host3.yml <<'EOF'
# host3: single 512GB NVMe SSD, VG rl_host3 has ~390GB free after root+swap.
# Leaves ~10GB headroom in the VG for future root growth. Note: the onboard
# NIC (enp2s0) is faulty - it only ever negotiated 100 Mb/s - so the static
# 10.10.10.30 now lives on a USB 2.5/1GbE adapter (NetworkManager profile
# `usb-eth`, MAC c8:a3:62:a1:cb:1d), which links at full speed and is fine for
# Longhorn replication. PXE reinstalls still go through the onboard enp2s0
# (its MAC is the one in bare-metal/hosts.csv / boot.ipxe), and the kickstart
# doesn't know about the USB adapter - the `usb-eth` profile would have to be
# recreated after a reinstall. kubelet's --node-ip is pinned to ansible_host
# (roles/kubeadm) because of this NIC move.
longhorn_lv_size_gb: 380
EOF
/bin/cat > ansible/inventory/host_vars/host2.yml <<'EOF'
# host2: single 512GB SATA SSD, VG rl_host2 has ~397GB free after root+swap.
# Leaves ~17GB headroom in the VG for future root growth.
#
# host2 is the tainted (NoSchedule) control-plane, and Longhorn's DaemonSets
# don't tolerate that taint - so this LV is carved but sits unused by
# Longhorn while host2 stays control-plane-only. Kept anyway so the node can
# be turned back into a storage-carrying worker without re-running a
# different storage layout.
longhorn_lv_size_gb: 380
EOF

/bin/cat > ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml <<'EOF'
---
- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  # No --cluster-name flag exists on `kubeadm init` (it's a ClusterConfiguration
  # field, only settable via --config) - naming the cluster would need a full
  # kubeadm config file for one cosmetic value, not worth it here.
  #
  # --control-plane-endpoint is a stable NAME (group_vars/all.yml), resolved
  # via /etc/hosts by the common role. kubeadm bakes it into the API server
  # cert and every kubeconfig (admin, kubelet, controller-manager, scheduler)
  # instead of this node's IP - so a future control-plane move doesn't need a
  # full rebuild. --apiserver-advertise-address pins the API server to the
  # LAN IP (not whatever interface holds the default route - same class of
  # bug as the kubelet --node-ip pin in roles/kubeadm). The cert SANs list
  # both the name and the IP explicitly: the IP because Cilium's
  # k8sServiceHost and the Mac's fetched kubeconfig use it directly.
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --control-plane-endpoint={{ control_plane_endpoint }}
    --apiserver-advertise-address={{ ansible_host }}
    --apiserver-cert-extra-sans={{ control_plane_endpoint_name }},{{ ansible_host }}
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
    {{ kubeadm_init_extra_args }}
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for foo user
  file:
    path: /home/foo/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: foo
    group: foo

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/foo/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: foo
    group: foo
    mode: "0600"

- name: Read admin kubeconfig
  slurp:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: admin_kubeconfig
  no_log: true

# admin.conf points at https://k8s-api.lab.local:6443. The Mac (jumpbox, over
# WireGuard or Tailscale) has no DNS for lab.local, so the local copy is
# rewritten to the control-plane's IP instead - it's in the API server cert's
# SANs, so TLS still verifies. Net effect: no /etc/hosts edit needed on the
# Mac. Written with copy (content-compared) rather than fetch + edit so a
# rerun on a healthy cluster stays at 0 changes.
#
# playbook_dir is ansible/playbooks/ - need two levels up to reach the repo
# root, not one (this previously landed at ansible/clusters/... and was never
# actually used by Terraform/kubectl at the documented path).
- name: Write kubeconfig to local machine (server rewritten to the control-plane IP)
  copy:
    content: >-
      {{ admin_kubeconfig.content | b64decode
         | replace('https://' ~ control_plane_endpoint,
                   'https://' ~ control_plane_ip ~ ':' ~ control_plane_endpoint_port) }}
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    mode: "0600"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false
  no_log: true

- name: Generate join command
  # Prints `kubeadm join k8s-api.lab.local:6443 ...` (the control-plane
  # endpoint, not this node's IP) - workers resolve it via the common role's
  # /etc/hosts entry.
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true

# host2 (Intel N150, 4c/4t, 16 GB) is the lightest node - it's a dedicated
# control-plane, so the standard kubeadm `NoSchedule` taint stays on and
# workloads land on host1/host3 (both 8c/16t Ryzen, 32 GB). kubeadm init
# already applies it; this just re-asserts it on every run in case someone
# untainted the node by hand (the old host1 layout removed it here).
#
# System DaemonSets that must run on every node already tolerate it: cilium
# + cilium-envoy (`operator: Exists`), metallb-speaker (explicit
# control-plane toleration - though kubeadm's
# node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers label keeps it
# from announcing LB IPs from here), and prometheus-node-exporter
# (`NoSchedule` + `Exists`). Longhorn's DaemonSets do NOT, by design - no
# volumes are attached on host2.
#
# kubelet registers the node under its OS hostname (kickstart sets
# `hostN.lab.local`, not the bare `hostN` used as the Ansible inventory
# name) - {{ inventory_hostname }} alone does not match any real node.
- name: Read control-plane node taints
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    get node {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local
    -o jsonpath={.spec.taints[*].key}
  register: cp_taints
  changed_when: false

- name: Keep control-plane NoSchedule taint (dedicated control-plane)
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    taint nodes {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local
    node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
  when: "'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' not in cp_taints.stdout.split()"
EOF
/bin/cat ansible/roles/kubeadm/tasks/main.yml | sed -n 1,60p

- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  # No --cluster-name flag exists on `kubeadm init` (it's a ClusterConfiguration
  # field, only settable via --config) - naming the cluster would need a full
  # kubeadm config file for one cosmetic value, not worth it here.
  #
  # --control-plane-endpoint is a stable NAME (group_vars/all.yml), resolved
  # via /etc/hosts by the common role. kubeadm bakes it into the API server
  # cert and every kubeconfig (admin, kubelet, controller-manager, scheduler)
  # instead of this node's IP - so a future control-plane move doesn't need a
  # full rebuild. --apiserver-advertise-address pins the API server to the
  # LAN IP (not whatever interface holds the default route - same class of
  # bug as the kubelet --node-ip pin in roles/kubeadm). The cert SANs list
  # both the name and the IP explicitly: the IP because Cilium's
  # k8sServiceHost and the Mac's fetched kubeconfig use it directly.
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --control-plane-endpoint={{ control_plane_endpoint }}
    --apiserver-advertise-address={{ ansible_host }}
    --apiserver-cert-extra-sans={{ control_plane_endpoint_name }},{{ ansible_host }}
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
    {{ kubeadm_init_extra_args }}
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for foo user
  file:
    path: /home/foo/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: foo
    group: foo

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/foo/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: foo
    group: foo
    mode: "0600"

- name: Read admin kubeconfig
  slurp:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: admin_kubeconfig
  no_log: true

# admin.conf points at https://k8s-api.lab.local:6443. The Mac (jumpbox, over
# WireGuard or Tailscale) has no DNS for lab.local, so the local copy is
# rewritten to the control-plane's IP instead - it's in the API server cert's
# SANs, so TLS still verifies. Net effect: no /etc/hosts edit needed on the
# Mac. Written with copy (content-compared) rather than fetch + edit so a
# rerun on a healthy cluster stays at 0 changes.
#
# playbook_dir is ansible/playbooks/ - need two levels up to reach the repo
# root, not one (this previously landed at ansible/clusters/... and was never
# actually used by Terraform/kubectl at the documented path).
- name: Write kubeconfig to local machine (server rewritten to the control-plane IP)
  copy:
    content: >-
      {{ admin_kubeconfig.content | b64decode
         | replace('https://' ~ control_plane_endpoint,
                   'https://' ~ control_plane_ip ~ ':' ~ control_plane_endpoint_port) }}
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    mode: "0600"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false
  no_log: true

- name: Generate join command
  # Prints `kubeadm join k8s-api.lab.local:6443 ...` (the control-plane
  # endpoint, not this node's IP) - workers resolve it via the common role's
  # /etc/hosts entry.
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true

# host2 (Intel N150, 4c/4t, 16 GB) is the lightest node - it's a dedicated
# control-plane, so the standard kubeadm `NoSchedule` taint stays on and
# workloads land on host1/host3 (both 8c/16t Ryzen, 32 GB). kubeadm init
# already applies it; this just re-asserts it on every run in case someone
# untainted the node by hand (the old host1 layout removed it here).
#
# System DaemonSets that must run on every node already tolerate it (checked
# live on the old cluster): cilium + cilium-envoy (`operator: Exists`),
# metallb-speaker (explicit control-plane toleration - though kubeadm's
# node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers label keeps it
# from announcing LB IPs from here), and prometheus-node-exporter
# (`NoSchedule` + `Exists`). Longhorn's DaemonSets do NOT tolerate it, by
# design - no workload volumes are attached on host2.
#
# kubelet registers the node under its OS hostname (kickstart sets
# `hostN.lab.local`, not the bare `hostN` used as the Ansible inventory
# name) - {{ inventory_hostname }} alone does not match any real node.
- name: Read control-plane node taints
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    get node {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local
    -o jsonpath={.spec.taints[*].key}
  register: cp_taints
  changed_when: false

- name: Keep control-plane NoSchedule taint (dedicated control-plane)
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    taint nodes {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local
    node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
  when: "'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' not in cp_taints.stdout.split()"

---
- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  # No --cluster-name flag exists on `kubeadm init` (it's a ClusterConfiguration
  # field, only settable via --config) - naming the cluster would need a full
  # kubeadm config file for one cosmetic value, not worth it here.
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for foo user
  file:
    path: /home/foo/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: foo
    group: foo

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/foo/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: foo
    group: foo
    mode: "0600"

- name: Fetch kubeconfig to local machine
  # playbook_dir is ansible/playbooks/ - need two levels up to reach the
  # repo root, not one (this previously landed at ansible/clusters/... and
  # was never actually used by Terraform/kubectl at the documented path).
  fetch:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    flat: true

- name: Restrict local kubeconfig permissions
  file:
    path: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    mode: "0600"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false

- name: Generate join command
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true

# host1 is the strongest node in this fleet (Ryzen 7 6800H, 1TB NVMe) -
# don't waste its capacity on etcd alone. Untainting is normal practice
# for a single-control-plane homelab cluster.
#
# kubelet registers the node under its OS hostname (kickstart sets
# `hostN.lab.local`, not the bare `hostN` used as the Ansible inventory
# name) - {{ inventory_hostname }} alone does not match any real node and
# silently no-ops here.
- name: Remove control-plane NoSchedule taint so this node is schedulable
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    taint nodes {{ inventory_hostname }}.lab.local node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule-
  register: untaint_result
  changed_when: "'untainted' in untaint_result.stdout"
  failed_when: untaint_result.rc != 0 and 'not found' not in untaint_result.stderr

---
- name: Add Kubernetes repo
  copy:
    dest: /etc/yum.repos.d/kubernetes.repo
    content: |
      [kubernetes]
      name=Kubernetes
      baseurl=https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{{ kubernetes_version }}/rpm/
      enabled=1
      gpgcheck=1
      gpgkey=https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{{ kubernetes_version }}/rpm/repodata/repomd.xml.key
      exclude=kubelet kubeadm kubectl cri-tools kubernetes-cni

- name: Install kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl
  dnf:
    name:
      - kubelet
      - kubeadm
      - kubectl
    state: present
    disable_excludes: kubernetes

- name: Install the dnf versionlock plugin
  # Not present on the minimal @core kickstart install (bare-metal/kickstart/) -
  # `dnf versionlock` fails with "No such command" without it.
  dnf:
    name: python3-dnf-plugin-versionlock
    state: present

- name: Hold kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl (dnf versionlock)
  command: dnf versionlock add {{ item }}
  loop:
    - kubelet
    - kubeadm
    - kubectl
  changed_when: false

- name: Pin kubelet node IP to the host's LAN address
  # Without --node-ip kubelet auto-detects its InternalIP from whatever
  # interface holds the default route. When host3's static IP moved to a USB
  # NIC (onboard port stuck at 100 Mb/s), kubelet briefly registered the
  # Cilium-internal 10.0.1.x address instead - pin it to ansible_host.
  copy:
    dest: /etc/sysconfig/kubelet
    content: "KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--node-ip={{ ansible_host }}\n"
  register: kubelet_sysconfig

- name: Restart kubelet to apply node IP
  systemd:
    name: kubelet
    state: restarted
  when: kubelet_sysconfig.changed

- name: Enable kubelet
  systemd:
    name: kubelet
    enabled: true

# k8s-homelab

A self-hosted Kubernetes cluster running on bare-metal mini PCs, managed entirely with Infrastructure as Code.

## Hardware

Actual fleet, polled live from each host (`lscpu`, `free -h`, `lsblk`, `dmidecode`) on 2026-08-11 - not
the original VM-template sizing:

| Host | IP | Board / model | CPU | RAM | Disk | NIC |
|------|----|----------------|-----|-----|------|-----|
| `host1` | 10.10.10.10 | Beelink SER-family (board `SER32001`) | AMD Ryzen 7 6800H - 8c/16t, up to 4.79 GHz | 32 GB | 1 TB NVMe (Samsung 970 EVO Plus) | 1 GbE (`eno1`), disabled onboard Wi-Fi (`wlp3s0`) |
| `host2` | 10.10.10.20 | Beelink Mini S-family (board `MINIS13001`) | Intel N150 - 4c/4t, up to 3.6 GHz | 16 GB | 512 GB SATA SSD | 1 GbE (`enp1s0`) |
| `host3` | 10.10.10.30 | generic OEM board (BIOS `5.19`) | AMD Ryzen 7 5800H - 8c/16t, up to 3.2 GHz | 32 GB | 512 GB NVMe SSD | `enp2s0` negotiated at only **100 Mb/s** (see note below), disabled onboard Wi-Fi (`wlp3s0`) |

Notes:
- **host1 and host3 are the two powerful nodes** (both 8c/16t AMD Ryzen mobile chips, 32 GB RAM), not
  `host3` alone - host1's CPU (6800H) is newer/faster than host3's (5800H) and its disk is 2x the size.
  `host2` (Intel N150, 4 threads, 16 GB) is clearly the lightest node. This corrects earlier internal notes
  that assumed host3 was "the beefiest" - it's mid-pack, not top.
- `host3`'s NIC is linking at 100 Mb/s instead of the expected 1 Gb/s - worth checking the cable/switch
  port before relying on it for anything storage- or throughput-sensitive (e.g. Longhorn replication).
- None of the three hosts have a second physical disk - each is a single-disk machine with one LVM volume
  group (`autopart --type=lvm --nohome` from the kickstart), root (70 GB) + swap, and several hundred GB of
  **unallocated free space in the VG** on every host. Any per-node storage (e.g. Longhorn) needs to come
  from a new LV carved out of that free space, not a dedicated `/dev/sdX` device.
- All three run Rocky Linux 9.8 "Blue Onyx", kernel `5.14.0-687.36.1.el9_8.x86_64`.

> This table used to describe the original Proxmox + VM template target (`n150-cp` control plane,
> `ser5-worker-1/2` workers at 10/28 vCPU/GB each). That design was abandoned - actual current fleet is 3
----
cd ansible
# Verify SSH connectivity
ansible -i inventory/hosts.yml all -m ping

# Bootstrap the full cluster
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml playbooks/bootstrap.yml
```

This carves Longhorn storage, installs containerd/kubeadm, initializes the control plane (host1), and
joins the workers (host2, host3). See [`docs/ansible.md`](docs/ansible.md) for details.

### 4. Terraform — install ArgoCD

```bash
cd terraform/cluster-bootstrap
terraform init
terraform apply
```

Installs ArgoCD and applies the `prod`/`stage` `AppProject`s and root Applications. See
[`docs/terraform.md`](docs/terraform.md).

### 5. ArgoCD takes over

ArgoCD automatically deploys Cilium, MetalLB, Longhorn, cert-manager, and ingress-nginx, then your
workloads under `apps/prod/` and `apps/stage/`.

> Sync Cilium first and wait for nodes to be `Ready` before the rest converges - see
> [`docs/argocd-gitops.md`](docs/argocd-gitops.md) for the full bootstrap flow and day-2 operations.

## Network

```
Home LAN: 192.168.2.0/24 -- Opal WAN side (DHCP)
                │
                │  WireGuard (wg_mgmt, udp/51821) - jumpbox management access
                ▼
Provisioning/production LAN: 10.10.10.0/24
  Opal (gateway/DHCP/TFTP/PXE): 10.10.10.1
  host1 (control-plane): 10.10.10.10
  host2 (worker):        10.10.10.20
  host3 (worker):        10.10.10.30
  MetalLB pool:           10.10.10.250-253

Ingress path:
  LAN → MetalLB IP (L2 ARP) → ingress-nginx → Pods
                                    (eBPF observed by Cilium/Hubble)
```

See [`docs/networking.md`](docs/networking.md) for MetalLB IP pool and Cilium configuration, and
[`bare-metal/README.md`](bare-metal/README.md) for the WireGuard tunnel and PXE network setup.

# k8s-homelab

A self-hosted Kubernetes cluster running on bare-metal mini PCs, managed entirely with Infrastructure as Code.

## Hardware

Actual fleet, polled live from each host (`lscpu`, `free -h`, `lsblk`, `dmidecode`) on 2026-08-11 - not
the original VM-template sizing:

| Host | IP | Board / model | CPU | RAM | Disk | NIC |
|------|----|----------------|-----|-----|------|-----|
| `host1` | 10.10.10.10 | Beelink SER-family (board `SER32001`) | AMD Ryzen 7 6800H - 8c/16t, up to 4.79 GHz | 32 GB | 1 TB NVMe (Samsung 970 EVO Plus) | 1 GbE (`eno1`), disabled onboard Wi-Fi (`wlp3s0`) |
| `host2` | 10.10.10.20 | Beelink Mini S-family (board `MINIS13001`) | Intel N150 - 4c/4t, up to 3.6 GHz | 16 GB | 512 GB SATA SSD | 1 GbE (`enp1s0`) |
| `host3` | 10.10.10.30 | generic OEM board (BIOS `5.19`) | AMD Ryzen 7 5800H - 8c/16t, up to 3.2 GHz | 32 GB | 512 GB NVMe SSD | USB 2.5/1GbE adapter (NM profile `usb-eth`, MAC `c8:a3:62:a1:cb:1d`) carries the static IP; onboard `enp2s0` is faulty (100 Mb/s only, see note below), disabled onboard Wi-Fi (`wlp3s0`) |

Notes:
- **host1 and host3 are the two powerful nodes** (both 8c/16t AMD Ryzen mobile chips, 32 GB RAM), not
  `host3` alone - host1's CPU (6800H) is newer/faster than host3's (5800H) and its disk is 2x the size.
  `host2` (Intel N150, 4 threads, 16 GB) is clearly the lightest node. This corrects earlier internal notes
  that assumed host3 was "the beefiest" - it's mid-pack, not top.
- `host3`'s onboard NIC (`enp2s0`) only ever negotiates 100 Mb/s - the port itself is faulty, not the
  cable/switch. The fix is a USB 2.5/1GbE adapter (NetworkManager profile `usb-eth`, MAC
  `c8:a3:62:a1:cb:1d`) that now holds the static `10.10.10.30` at full speed. PXE reinstalls still go
  through the onboard `enp2s0` (its MAC is the one in `bare-metal/hosts.csv`), and the kickstart doesn't
  configure the USB adapter - recreate the `usb-eth` profile after a reinstall. kubelet's `--node-ip` is
  pinned by Ansible (`roles/kubeadm`) because this NIC move once made it pick a Cilium IP.
- **Cluster roles follow the hardware:** `host2`, the lightest node, is the dedicated control-plane (keeps
  the standard `NoSchedule` taint); `host1` and `host3` are the workers that run workloads.
- None of the three hosts have a second physical disk - each is a single-disk machine with one LVM volume
  group (`autopart --type=lvm --nohome` from the kickstart), root (70 GB) + swap, and several hundred GB of
  **unallocated free space in the VG** on every host. Any per-node storage (e.g. Longhorn) needs to come
  from a new LV carved out of that free space, not a dedicated `/dev/sdX` device.
- All three run Rocky Linux 9.8 "Blue Onyx", kernel `5.14.0-687.36.1.el9_8.x86_64`.

> This table used to describe the original Proxmox + VM template target (`n150-cp` control plane,
> `ser5-worker-1/2` workers at 10/28 vCPU/GB each). That design was abandoned - actual current fleet is 3
> bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 hosts (host1/host2/host3), no hypervisor anywhere - see the Note below.

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| Hypervisor | none - bare-metal |
| OS | Rocky Linux 9 (kickstart, bare-metal) |
| Container runtime | containerd |
| Kubernetes | kubeadm 1.31 |
| CNI | Cilium (eBPF) |
| Load balancer | MetalLB (L2) |
| Ingress | ingress-nginx |
| Storage | Longhorn (LVM-carved LVs, no dedicated disk) |
| TLS | cert-manager |
| Monitoring | kube-prometheus-stack (Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager) |
| GitOps | ArgoCD (app-of-apps, prod/stage split via AppProjects) |

# Ansible — Cluster Bootstrap

Ansible configures the OS and bootstraps Kubernetes on the three bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 hosts. It is
idempotent — safe to rerun. Run from the jumpbox, over the WireGuard tunnel into `10.10.10.0/24`
(`bare-metal/README.md`, "Tunnel WireGuard pour le jumpbox").

## Prerequisites

```bash
pip install ansible
ansible-galaxy collection install ansible.posix community.general
```

SSH access as `foo` (kickstart-created user, root login locked) with `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab` — both
already set as defaults in `ansible/ansible.cfg`.

## Inventory

`ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` defines the three nodes:

```
control_plane: host1 (10.10.10.10)
workers:       host2 (10.10.10.20)
               host3 (10.10.10.30)
```

host1 was chosen as control-plane because live hardware polling showed it's the strongest node (Ryzen 7
6800H, 1TB NVMe) — not the convention of putting the lightest node on the control-plane. See the top-level
README's hardware table.

## Configuration

Key variables in `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`:

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `kubernetes_version` | `1.31` | Minor version for the kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl repo |
| `pod_cidr` | `10.244.0.0/16` | Pod network range |
| `service_cidr` | `10.96.0.0/12` | Service network range |
| `kube_proxy_enabled` | `false` | Cilium replaces kube-proxy |
| `ansible_user` | `foo` | Kickstart-created user; root login is locked |

There's no `--cluster-name` flag on `kubeadm init` (it's a `ClusterConfiguration` field, only settable via
a full `--config` file) — not worth introducing one just to name the cluster "homelab" cosmetically.

Per-host `longhorn_lv_size_gb` in `ansible/host_vars/{host1,host2,host3}.yml` — sized from each host's real
free LVM space (see `docs/storage.md`).

## Running the Full Bootstrap

```bash
cd ansible
ansible-playbook playbooks/bootstrap.yml
```

Execution order:
1. **common** (all nodes) — swap off, kernel modules, sysctl, open-iscsi
2. **storage** (all nodes) — carve an LV from free VG space, mount at `/var/lib/longhorn`
3. **containerd** (all nodes) — install, configure `SystemdCgroup=true`
4. **kubeadm** (all nodes) — install kubelet/kubeadm/kubectl, hold versions
5. **control-plane** (host1) — `kubeadm init`, remove the control-plane `NoSchedule` taint (host1 is the
   strongest node — don't waste its capacity on etcd alone), fetch kubeconfig to
   `clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`
6. **worker** (host2, host3) — `kubeadm join`

## After Bootstrap

The kubeconfig is written to `clusters/homelab/kubeconfig` (gitignored — it's a live cluster-admin
credential, this repo is public). Use it locally:

### storage
- None of the three hosts have a second disk — each is single-disk (`autopart --type=lvm --nohome` from
  the kickstart) with substantial free space left in its LVM volume group after root+swap
- Carves an LV (`lv_longhorn`, sized per-host in `ansible/host_vars/`) out of that free space, formats
  XFS, mounts at `/var/lib/longhorn`

### containerd
- Adds Docker CE's `centos` yum repo (provides `containerd.io` for Rocky Linux)
- Generates default config then patches `SystemdCgroup = true`
- **Do not regenerate the config manually** — this setting will revert to `false` and kubelet will refuse to start

### control-plane
- Runs `kubeadm init --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy`
- `kube-proxy` is intentionally skipped — Cilium handles service routing via eBPF
- Removes the control-plane `NoSchedule` taint — host1 is the strongest node in the fleet, not just an
  etcd appliance
- Generates a join token and stores it as a fact for the worker play
- Fetches `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf` to your local `clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`

### worker
- Runs the join command generated by the control-plane play
- Labels the node with `node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=worker`

## Upgrading Kubernetes

See `docs/day2-operations.md` for the full upgrade procedure.

# Storage — Longhorn

Longhorn provides distributed block storage across all three nodes (host1 is untainted/schedulable too,
not etcd-only — see `docs/ansible.md`). It is the default `StorageClass`.

## How it Works

None of the three hosts have a second physical disk — each is single-disk, so Longhorn does **not** manage
a raw block device directly here (unlike the original VM-template design, which assumed a dedicated
`/dev/sdb`). Instead, the Ansible `storage` role (`ansible/roles/storage/`) carves a dedicated LV out of
each host's otherwise-unallocated LVM free space, formats it XFS, and mounts it at `/var/lib/longhorn`
*before* Kubernetes/Longhorn ever gets involved — Longhorn just sees a normal, already-mounted filesystem
path on each node. Per-host LV sizes (`ansible/host_vars/{host1,host2,host3}.yml`) come from real
`lsblk`/`vgs` polling, not an assumption:

| Host | LV size | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| host1 | 800 GB | 1TB NVMe, ~846GB was free in the VG |
| host2 | 380 GB | 512GB SATA SSD, ~397GB was free in the VG |
| host3 | 380 GB | 512GB NVMe, ~390GB was free in the VG — **NIC currently links at only 100 Mb/s**, fix the cable/switch port before relying on this node for replica placement, replication over 100 Mb will bottleneck |

With `defaultReplicaCount: 2` (`clusters/homelab/infrastructure/longhorn.yml`) across three nodes, every
volume is replicated onto two of the three — one node going down does not cause data loss.

## Using Longhorn (PVCs)

Any `PersistentVolumeClaim` without an explicit `storageClassName` uses Longhorn by default:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1

## What to Watch

- Longhorn volumes become `Degraded` if a replica is unavailable (node down, disk full). They recover
  automatically when the replica comes back.
- Disk pressure: Longhorn reserves `storageMinimalAvailablePercentage: 10` — it will stop scheduling new
  replicas when less than 10% disk is free.
- host3's degraded NIC link (100 Mb/s instead of 1 Gb/s) will slow replica rebuilds/writes to that node
  specifically — worth fixing before leaning on this cluster for anything storage-heavy.

you need one of:

- **On the Opal's own LAN** (physically connected or on its Wi-Fi) — nothing else needed.
- **On the home network** — bring up the WireGuard tunnel first:
  ```bash
  sudo wg-quick up ~/.wireguard-homelab/mac-jumpbox.conf
  ```
  See `bare-metal/README.md`, "Tunnel WireGuard pour le jumpbox", for initial setup if this doesn't exist
  yet. Tear down with `sudo wg-quick down ~/.wireguard-homelab/mac-jumpbox.conf` when done.
- **From anywhere** — Tailscale, connected to the same tailnet as `host1-homelab` (a subnet router for
  `10.10.10.0/24`, set up via `ansible/roles/tailscale/`). No manual up/down needed once connected. See
  `bare-metal/README.md`, "Tailscale", for setup and two gotchas: the advertised route needs manual
  approval in the Tailscale admin console (silent failure otherwise — the machine shows "Connected" but
  nothing behind it routes), and a commercial VPN client (e.g. NordVPN) running at the same time on the
  jumpbox blocks the subnet route even after approval — disable it first if `ping 10.10.10.10` isn't
  working despite everything else looking right.

Verify with `ping 10.10.10.1` (the Opal) before troubleshooting anything else, whichever path you used.

## Connecting with kubectl

The admin kubeconfig is fetched to `clusters/homelab/kubeconfig` by Ansible's control-plane role (gitignored
— it's a live cluster-admin credential, never commit it). Point `KUBECONFIG` at it:

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/k8s-homelab/clusters/homelab/kubeconfig
kubectl get nodes
```

Or merge it into your default `~/.kube/config` if you prefer not to export the var every session:
```bash
KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:/path/to/k8s-homelab/clusters/homelab/kubeconfig kubectl config view --flatten > /tmp/merged && mv /tmp/merged ~/.kube/config
kubectl config use-context kubernetes-admin@kubernetes
```

If this file is missing or you suspect it's stale (e.g. after `kubeadm certs renew`), re-fetch it — see
`docs/ansible.md` or `docs/day2-operations.md` ("Rotating Kubernetes Certificates").

Note: `kubectl get nodes` shows `host1.lab.local` / `host2.lab.local` / `host3.lab.local` — the OS
hostname kubelet registers under, not the bare `host1`/`host2`/`host3` used elsewhere in this repo
(Ansible inventory, `hosts.csv`). Any `kubectl label`/`taint`/`describe node` command needs the
`.lab.local` suffix.

## SSH to the hosts directly

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10   # host1, control-plane
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.20   # host2, worker
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.30   # host3, worker
```

`foo` is the kickstart-created user (root login is locked, key-only auth, passwordless sudo via
`%wheel`). Add an SSH config `Host` block if typing the key path every time is annoying:

```
Host host1 host2 host3
  User foo
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab
```

Prefer fixing things through the repo (Ansible/manifests) and redeploying over ad hoc SSH changes — see
### 1. Update the target version

In `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`:
```yaml
kubernetes_version: "1.32"
```

### 2. Upgrade the control plane (host1)

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10

# Update the repo to the new minor version (already done via group_vars + Ansible)
# Or manually edit /etc/yum.repos.d/kubernetes.repo baseurl to v1.32

# Upgrade kubeadm
sudo dnf install -y --disableexcludes=kubernetes kubelet-1.32.* kubectl-1.32.*
sudo dnf versionlock delete kubelet kubectl
sudo dnf versionlock add kubelet kubectl
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
```

### 3. Upgrade each worker (one at a time)

```bash
# From your local machine — drain the node
kubectl drain host2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# SSH into the worker
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.20
sudo dnf install -y --disableexcludes=kubernetes kubeadm-1.32.* kubelet-1.32.* kubectl-1.32.*
sudo dnf versionlock delete kubeadm kubelet kubectl
sudo dnf versionlock add kubeadm kubelet kubectl
sudo kubeadm upgrade node
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# From local — uncordon
kubectl uncordon host2
```

Repeat for `host3` (10.10.10.30).

---

## Rotating Kubernetes Certificates

Certificates created by kubeadm expire after 1 year. Check expiry:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
```

Renew all certs:
```bash
sudo kubeadm certs renew all
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Regenerate kubeconfig (new cert embedded)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf.bak
sudo kubeadm kubeconfig user --client-name admin > /tmp/admin.conf
sudo mv /tmp/admin.conf /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
```

Then re-fetch the kubeconfig locally:
```bash
scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10:/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf clusters/homelab/kubeconfig
```

---

## Adding a Worker Node

There's no VM layer to provision through Terraform anymore — a new node means new physical hardware:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@<host-ip> sudo reboot
# Wait for node to come back
kubectl uncordon <node>
```

Verify the host's boot order still prioritizes the local disk before rebooting anything with PXE enabled
— `bare-metal/README.md` documents the host2 reinstall-loop incident this caused once already.

---

## Backing Up etcd

kubeadm clusters store all cluster state in etcd on the control plane (host1).

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10

sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Verify
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).db --write-out=table
```

Copy the snapshot off the node:
```bash
scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10:/tmp/etcd-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).db ./backups/
```

---

## Rebuilding the Cluster from Scratch

There's no VM layer to tear down/recreate — "from scratch" means re-running kubeadm on the same hosts:

```bash
# Reset kubeadm state on every host (control plane first, then workers)
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.10 sudo kubeadm reset -f
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.20 sudo kubeadm reset -f
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab foo@10.10.10.30 sudo kubeadm reset -f

# Re-bootstrap
cd ansible
